premise: A client conforms at profile P if, driven exactly as a third-party consumer would drive it, it passes every case in P with no unsupported result and no error. The other 13 decisions are SETTLED - every client obeys them now - and they keep their cases so a regression turns them red again rather than passing unnoticed.

cases.title: canonText over ascii
cases.why: The length prefix is what makes the encoding injective, and it counts code points: plain ASCII, the case every implementation gets right. A client using a UTF-16 or byte length writes a different document for the same payload.

groups.note: canonOptional, canonList and canonFields. Every document is a canonFields, so the field sort and the ASCII field-name restriction that makes it language-independent live here.

cases.title: canonOptional of None
cases.why: None encodes as an empty optional rather than being omitted, so a document with an absent field still differs from a document that never had the field at all.

cases.title: canonOptional of Some
cases.why: The inner value is canonicalised before it is wrapped, so the optional carries a length over an already-tagged string and not over the raw payload.

cases.title: canonOptional of Some with an empty inner value
cases.why: This is the documented non-injectivity: Some "" and None both encode a zero-length payload under a different length, and pinning it now stops a future document from inheriting the ambiguity unnoticed.
cases.note: Not reachable from any shipped document. Pinned so that the first document to use canonOptional has to look at this case.

cases.title: canonList of an empty list
cases.why: An empty list still encodes its element count and the trailing colon; a client that emits nothing at all collides with a list whose single element is empty.

cases.title: canonList of two elements
cases.why: The element separator is a pipe and the count is inside the encoded value, which is what stops two different lists from producing the same bytes.

cases.title: canonList of one element
cases.why: A single-element list must still carry its count, otherwise it would be indistinguishable from the bare element in a nested position.

cases.title: canonList of one element that itself contains a pipe
cases.why: Without the leading count this would encode identically to a two-element list, which is the exact ambiguity the count exists to prevent; this case and the next must produce different bytes.

cases.title: canonList of the two elements a and b
cases.why: Paired with the previous case: same characters after the count, different count, therefore different bytes. A client that drops the count passes both cases individually and fails the pair.
cases.note: Deliberately the same input as canon-list-two-elements; the pair is the assertion.

cases.title: canonList is order sensitive
cases.why: Lists are positional and are never sorted, unlike record fields; a client that normalises list order changes the digest of every entry document that carries allocations or plays.

cases.title: canonList over already-canonical elements
cases.why: The caller canonicalises the elements, not canonList; passing raw payloads instead of canonical fragments produces shorter bytes that no other client would reproduce.

cases.title: canonList whose elements are bare canonFields values
cases.why: Trade Wars allocations and Pixel Race plays nest records inside a list with no schema wrapper; a client that wraps each element in a document instead produces a different entry digest for the same play.

cases.title: canonFields of no fields
cases.why: The empty record is the base of every empty document, including merkleEmpty, so an implementation that emits nothing here gets a different empty-period root.

cases.title: canonFields sorts by field name, not by insertion order
cases.why: Source order must not reach the digest, otherwise adding a field in a later version of a builder would silently change a v1 document that the ledger already committed to.

cases.title: canonFields of the same two fields already in order
cases.why: Paired with the previous case: the two must produce identical bytes, which is the actual claim. Either case alone would pass an implementation that never sorts.

cases.title: canonFields sorts A before a
cases.why: The sort is code-point order, so uppercase comes first; a case-folding or locale-aware comparator reverses this pair and changes the digest of any document mixing cases in its field names.

cases.title: Duplicate field names are kept in insertion order, not rejected

cases.title: An amount far outside the band is refused

groups.note: The document envelope: scheme prefix, one literal pipe, schema, version, fields. The digest is the sha256 of that text as raw UTF-8, which is what makes plain sha256sum a check.

cases.title: The smallest possible document
cases.why: This pins the envelope with nothing inside it: one literal pipe after the prefix and no separator at all between schema, version and fields. A client that inserts a separator changes every document in the scheme at once.

cases.title: The only literal pipe is the one after the scheme prefix
cases.why: Every other pipe in a document belongs to a canonList and is inside a length-prefixed value; a stray separator anywhere else would make the prefix ambiguous for a reader splitting on the first pipe.

cases.title: The schema name is part of the hashed text
cases.why: Two payload types with the same fields must not collide; the schema is what separates a Merkle node from an audit row and makes claiming leaf-hood a sha256 collision problem rather than a formatting trick.

cases.title: The schema version is part of the hashed text
cases.why: A v2 of a schema must not be able to produce a v1 digest; pinning version 2 of the same schema next to version 1 shows the two are distinguishable without reading the fields.

cases.title: Field order inside a document does not reach the digest
cases.why: A builder that appends a field at the end rather than in sorted position would otherwise produce a document the ledger cannot reproduce; this is the composed form of the canonFields sort.

cases.title: textDigest of arccade matches plain sha256sum
cases.why: The value of the whole scheme is that a third party can run sha256sum over the published document and get the number on the ledger; if this one drifts, that claim is gone.
cases.note: Reproducible from a shell with: printf 'arccade' | sha256sum

cases.title: The digest is over UTF-8 bytes, not UTF-16 code units
cases.why: An implementation hashing UTF-16 or Latin-1 bytes agrees with everyone on ASCII and diverges the moment a document carries a non-ASCII venue name or tier.

cases.title: textDigest of the empty string is refused
cases.why: Daml's toHex "" is a runtime error, so Daml cannot produce this digest at all; a client that returns e3b0c442... computes a value the ledger never can, and documentDigest can never reach the case because every document starts with the scheme prefix.

cases.title: The digest of the smallest document is pinned alongside its text
cases.why: Pinning only the digest hides which byte moved; pinning only the text lets a hashing bug through. Every document-producing case in this suite pins both, and a runner must report which of the two failed.

groups.note: Tree construction. A lone trailing node is PROMOTED unchanged, never paired with itself, which is what keeps [a,b,c] and [a,b,c,c] from sharing a root (CVE-2012-2459).

cases.title: The empty-period root
cases.why: A day with zero cycles is still anchored, otherwise "nothing happened" and "we did not report" are indistinguishable; this constant is on the ledger in the live TestNet anchor for 2026-08-27.

cases.title: An internal node over the first two golden leaves
cases.why: Internal nodes hash under a different schema from leaves, and this is the constant that binds that separation across the four implementations.

cases.title: The three-leaf golden root
cases.why: Three leaves is the smallest tree with a promotion in it, so this single constant covers both the pairing rule and the promotion rule that CVE-2012-2459 is about.

cases.title: A node over two identical children is not the child
cases.why: The leaf and node schemas differ, so no hashing of children can ever collide with a leaf value; a client that hashes the concatenation of children instead loses that separation and an internal node can be presented as a cycle.

cases.title: Swapping the two children changes the node
cases.why: Proof folding depends on knowing which side the sibling was on; a commutative node would let a forged proof place a sibling on either side and still verify.

cases.title: merkleRoot of no leaves is the empty root
cases.why: A client that returns an all-zero hash or throws for an empty period cannot anchor a quiet day, and the anchor for a quiet day is exactly the one an auditor most needs.

cases.title: A single leaf IS the root, unwrapped
cases.why: A client that wraps a lone leaf in a node produces a root nobody else computes for a one-cycle day, which is the most common non-empty period a small venue has.

cases.title: The promoted leaf 2 of 3 verifies against the root
cases.why: The step list for a promoted leaf is shorter than ceil(log2 3); folding it still has to reach the root, which is what proves the promotion rule is consistent between the builder and the verifier.

cases.title: The promoted leaf 4 of 5 verifies against the root
cases.why: The step list for a promoted leaf is shorter than ceil(log2 5); folding it still has to reach the root, which is what proves the promotion rule is consistent between the builder and the verifier.

cases.title: The promoted leaf 8 of 9 verifies against the root
cases.why: The step list for a promoted leaf is shorter than ceil(log2 9); folding it still has to reach the root, which is what proves the promotion rule is consistent between the builder and the verifier.

pins.daml: merkleVerify (leafN 9) (merkleProof 8 [leafN 1, leafN 2, leafN 3, leafN 4, leafN 5, leafN 6, leafN 7, leafN 8, leafN 9]) (merkleRoot [leafN 1, leafN 2, leafN 3, leafN 4, leafN 5, leafN 6, leafN 7, leafN 8, leafN 9]) === "true"

cases.title: An out-of-range index yields an empty proof, not an exception
cases.why: All four implementations return an empty list rather than throwing, and callers rely on it; the danger is the next case, so this behaviour has to be pinned before it can be reasoned about.

cases.title: An empty proof verifies anything against a single-leaf tree
cases.why: merkleVerify with no steps reduces to leaf == root, so an out-of-range index against a one-leaf tree "verifies"; range-check before trusting an empty proof, and never expose bare merkleVerify as the auditor API.

cases.title: A proof for one leaf does not verify a different leaf
cases.why: Without this the whole group could be satisfied by an implementation that returns true unconditionally, and every proof case above would be worthless.

cases.title: Flipping a sibling in the proof breaks verification
cases.why: The proof is the thing an auditor is handed, so the case where the proof rather than the leaf is wrong needs its own assertion.

pins.daml: merkleVerify (leafN 0) (map (\s -> s with sibling = leafN 9) (merkleProof 0 [leafN 1, leafN 2, leafN 3])) (merkleRoot [leafN 1, leafN 2, leafN 3]) === "false"

cases.title: Flipping which side a sibling sits on breaks verification
cases.why: siblingOnLeft is the only thing distinguishing two otherwise identical proofs, and a client that ignores it verifies a leaf that is not in the tree at the claimed position.

pins.daml: merkleVerify (leafN 1) (map (\s -> s with siblingOnLeft = not s.siblingOnLeft) (merkleProof 0 [leafN 1, leafN 2, leafN 3])) (merkleRoot [leafN 1, leafN 2, leafN 3]) === "false"

cases.title: Folding a proof yields the root as a value, not a boolean
cases.why: When a proof fails, the folded value is the only thing that says how far it got; a client that only exposes the boolean leaves an auditor with no way to tell a wrong leaf from a wrong sibling.

cases.title: Folding an empty proof returns the leaf unchanged
cases.why: This is the arithmetic behind the single-leaf trap above, stated as a value rather than a boolean so the reason the trap exists is visible.

groups.note: The fifteen fields of arccade.cycle-audit-row. Amounts go in as canonInt (integer 1e-10 units), NOT canonDecimal; the two timestamps go in as canonInt, NOT canonTimeMicros, even though they are times.

cases.title: The Daml golden audit row and its leaf
cases.why: This is the constant that binds the Daml, JavaScript, Python and Java leaf builders to one another; an auditor verifies a proof in JavaScript or Python, never in Daml, so if this drifts the proof stops meaning anything.

cases.title: The leaf of TestNet row 0 (tw-testnet-1787437747)
cases.why: test-vectors/cycle-rows.json is already the cross-language contract for what the ledger emitted; lifting row 0 in as a typed input means a client that cannot read transaction trees still has to prove it hashes the row identically.

cases.title: Amount fields carry the i tag, never the d tag
cases.why: The row already holds integer 1e-10 units, so running them through canonDecimal would multiply by 1e10 a second time; the pinned text is where an implementer can see the tag and check it by eye.

cases.title: Timestamp fields carry the i tag, never the m tag
cases.why: Both timestamps are microsecond times but the row encodes them with canonInt; a client that reaches for canonTimeMicros because the field name ends in Micros produces a leaf that differs from the ledger in exactly two places.

cases.title: A row carrying the returned-in-full disposition tag

cases.title: Commit and closing are joined by the stake contract id
cases.why: The closing choice never repeats the cycleId, so a reader that tries to join on it finds nothing; the commit exercise result is the only link between the two halves in the stream.

cases.title: An aborted cycle derives its amounts rather than reading them
cases.why: GameStake_Abort carries only a reason, so the amounts have to come from the mechanic: unlocking a TimeLockedHolding pays the owner in full and this mechanic cannot forfeit, which is why the stake comes back and nothing else moves.

cases.title: An expired cycle derives its amounts from nothing at all
cases.why: GameStake_ExpireUnsettled carries no argument whatsoever, so a reader that expects a disposition in the choice argument produces no row and the cycle vanishes from the period it belongs to.

cases.title: An aborted cycle still produces a row
cases.why: Its outcomeDigest is empty because no outcome ever existed, not because the reader failed to find one; a reader that skips rows with no outcome removes exactly the cycles a player would complain about.

cases.title: A commit with no closing is reported, not dropped
cases.why: An open cycle belongs to no period yet, but a reader that discards it silently cannot tell an open cycle from one whose closing it failed to parse, and those are very different facts about a venue.

cases.title: A closing whose commit is outside the window is reported
cases.why: A window boundary always cuts some cycle in half; surfacing the orphan is what lets a report say which period the missing commit belongs to instead of leaving a settled cycle unaccounted for.

cases.title: A settlement whose unlock rides along and agrees raises no warning
cases.why: When the unlock is in the same transaction the created Amulet gives an independent reading of what was returned; the agreeing case has to be pinned or the disagreeing one below could be satisfied by a client that always warns.

cases.title: A stated return that disagrees with the unlock is reported
cases.why: The choice argument is what the venue says and the unlocked Amulet is what actually moved; reporting the disagreement rather than trusting the argument is the difference between a report and a press release.
cases.note: The live fixture contains no such case, which is why this one is synthetic; the warning path would otherwise be unexercised.

groups.note: The tie-break. cycle-rows.json says "committedAtMicros, then cycleId" without naming a collation, so today neither localeCompare nor UTF-16 compareTo is wrong and two honest implementations produce two different Merkle roots over the same set of cycles. This group picks code-point order.

cases.title: Tie-break between "B" and "a"
cases.why: Leaf order decides the root, so a collation difference is a different published root over the same cycles; an uppercase letter against a lowercase one is a pair where locale collation, UTF-16 code-unit order and code-point order do not all agree.

cases.title: Tie-break between "c-1" and "C-1"
cases.why: Leaf order decides the root, so a collation difference is a different published root over the same cycles; the same id differing only in case is a pair where locale collation, UTF-16 code-unit order and code-point order do not all agree.

cases.title: Tie-break between "x_1" and "x-1"
cases.why: Leaf order decides the root, so a collation difference is a different published root over the same cycles; underscore against hyphen, which locale collation often treats as equivalent is a pair where locale collation, UTF-16 code-unit order and code-point order do not all agree.

cases.title: Tie-break between "_z" and "az"
cases.why: Leaf order decides the root, so a collation difference is a different published root over the same cycles; a leading punctuation character, which many collations ignore entirely is a pair where locale collation, UTF-16 code-unit order and code-point order do not all agree.

cases.title: Tie-break between "🎮" and "�"
cases.why: Leaf order decides the root, so a collation difference is a different published root over the same cycles; an astral code point against the replacement character, which UTF-16 compareTo orders backwards is a pair where locale collation, UTF-16 code-unit order and code-point order do not all agree.

cases.title: Tie-break between "1a" and "a1"
cases.why: Leaf order decides the root, so a collation difference is a different published root over the same cycles; a digit against a letter at the first position is a pair where locale collation, UTF-16 code-unit order and code-point order do not all agree.

cases.title: Tie-break between "ab" and "abc"
cases.why: Leaf order decides the root, so a collation difference is a different published root over the same cycles; one id that is a prefix of the other is a pair where locale collation, UTF-16 code-unit order and code-point order do not all agree.

cases.title: A later commit sorts after an earlier one whatever the ids say
cases.why: The tie-break only applies when the timestamps are equal; a client that sorts by cycleId first reorders every period and the tie-break cases above would not catch it.

cases.title: One microsecond is enough to separate two commits
cases.why: If a client truncates commit times to milliseconds these two collapse into a tie and fall through to the cycleId comparison, which reverses them; the tie-break and the timestamp precision are the same bug seen twice.

groups.note: The validators. Only the JavaScript client has them, which is precisely why they need cases: a Java backend that accepts a cycleId the JavaScript client refuses writes a custody tag the auditor's tooling cannot parse.

cases.title: A plain cycle id is accepted
cases.why: Every rejection case below is only meaningful next to an acceptance; without this one a client that refuses everything would pass the whole group.

cases.title: An id of 64 ASCII characters is accepted
cases.why: Sixty-four is the limit, and the accepting edge has to be pinned separately from the rejecting one or an off-by-one in either direction goes unnoticed.

cases.title: An id of 65 characters is refused
cases.why: The limit exists because the id goes inside a custody tag the ledger stores; one character over is the case that says the check is a comparison and not a formality.

cases.title: An empty id is refused
cases.why: An empty cycleId produces a custody tag with two adjacent colons that parses back into a different pair of components, so the lock could no longer be matched to its cycle.

cases.title: An id containing a colon is refused
cases.why: Colon separates the fields of the custody tag, so an id containing one makes the tag ambiguous and an auditor splitting it recovers a cycleId and an entryDigest that were never written.

cases.title: An id containing a pipe is refused
cases.why: Pipe is the canonList element separator, so an id carrying one can reshape any list a report puts it in even though the custody tag itself would survive.

cases.title: An id of 64 astral code points is accepted
cases.why: Daml T.length counts code points, so the ledger accepts this id; the JavaScript check counts UTF-16 units, sees 128 and refuses, which means the auditor path breaks on a cycle the ledger already committed.

cases.title: An id of 65 astral code points is refused
cases.why: The limit is in code points on both sides of the boundary; without this case D2 could be satisfied by removing the length check altogether.

cases.title: A generated uuid-shaped id is accepted
cases.why: newCycleId produces exactly this shape, so the validator and the generator have to agree or every id the SDK produces would be refused by its own check.

cases.title: A lowercase 64-character hash is accepted
cases.why: Digests are the join between a document and the ledger, and this is the shape every one of them has; the rejections below only mean something with the acceptance pinned.

cases.title: An uppercase hash is refused
cases.why: Case is not normalised anywhere in the scheme, so an uppercase digest inside a custody tag produces a different tag and the settlement check against it fails at the worst moment.

cases.title: A 63-character hash is refused
cases.why: A truncated digest is what a copy-paste through a spreadsheet produces, and it would otherwise sit in a custody tag looking almost right.

cases.title: A 65-character hash is refused
cases.why: The other side of the length check, which a regex anchored only at the start would let through.

cases.title: A hash with a non-hex character is refused
cases.why: A digest with a stray character is not a digest, and accepting it would let a custody tag exist that no document can ever produce.

cases.title: An empty hash is refused
cases.why: The empty string is what an unset field looks like, and it is the value most likely to reach the check by accident.

cases.title: A plain trade id is accepted
cases.why: Trade ids follow the same rules as cycle ids because they go into the same kind of tag; pinning the acceptance keeps the two validators from drifting apart.

cases.title: A trade id containing a pipe is refused
cases.why: The v1 trade document joins its components with pipes and has no length prefixes, so an id carrying one silently reshapes the document.

cases.title: A 65-character trade id is refused
cases.why: Same bound as the cycle id, and pinned separately because the two checks are separate code paths that have already drifted once.

cases.title: A tenant id with a slash is refused
cases.why: Tenant ids are the namespace prefix that keeps one tenant from minting another tenant's item under the same registry party, so a slash decides whether two tenants can collide.

cases.title: A namespaced instrument id is tenant slash local
cases.why: Slash was chosen because colon and pipe are both meaningful in the digest encoding; a client that picks a different separator produces ids that parse back into the wrong tenant.

cases.title: Parsing a namespaced instrument id back into its parts
cases.why: Isolation checks depend on this parse, so a client that splits on the last slash instead of the first attributes an item to the wrong tenant.

cases.title: An instrument id with no namespace parses to a null tenant
cases.why: Ecosystem-wide assets such as Amulet have no tenant prefix; a client that treats the whole id as a tenant name refuses every Canton Coin leg in the SDK.

cases.title: A local id containing a slash is refused
cases.why: A second slash makes the parse ambiguous, and the ambiguity resolves in favour of the tenant prefix, so an item could be minted that reads back as belonging to someone else.

cases.title: A local id containing a colon is refused
cases.why: Colon is the tag separator in every custody, trade and transfer tag the SDK writes, so an id carrying one produces a tag that cannot be parsed back.

cases.title: A 97-character local id is refused here too
cases.why: This bound is checked in a second place with a second message, and the two have to stay in step or an item name accepted by one entry point is refused by the other.

groups.note: arccade-game-sdk:1:<cycleId>:<entryDigest>. The tag is what binds a real ledger lock to a particular cycle and its entry commitment; a generic string in optContext makes the stake unsettleable.

cases.title: The custody tag is prefix, cycle id, digest
cases.why: Settlement re-derives this string and compares it to what is in the lock, so a client that assembles it differently produces a stake that can only ever be aborted.

cases.title: The custody tag of TestNet row 0
cases.why: These three tags are on the ledger inside real locks, so reproducing them from the cycle id and entry digest is the check that the client's tag builder matches what was actually written.

cases.title: The custody tag of TestNet row 1
cases.why: These three tags are on the ledger inside real locks, so reproducing them from the cycle id and entry digest is the check that the client's tag builder matches what was actually written.

cases.title: The custody tag of TestNet row 2
cases.why: These three tags are on the ledger inside real locks, so reproducing them from the cycle id and entry digest is the check that the client's tag builder matches what was actually written.

cases.title: The custody tag prefix is a wire constant
cases.why: Renaming it would orphan every lock already on the ledger, because settlement compares the stored optContext against a freshly built tag.

cases.title: A cycle id with a colon cannot become a tag
cases.why: The tag has four colon-separated parts, so an id containing one produces a five-part string that an auditor splits into a cycle id and a digest neither of which was written.

cases.title: A non-hex entry digest cannot become a tag
cases.why: The digest half of the tag is what binds the lock to the entry document; a value that is not a sha256 at all means there is no document it could ever be checked against.

cases.title: An uppercase entry digest cannot become a tag
cases.why: Case is never normalised, so an uppercase digest builds a tag that differs from the one settlement re-derives even though both spell the same hash.

cases.title: An empty cycle id cannot become a tag
cases.why: It would produce two adjacent colons, and a parser splitting the tag would read the digest as the cycle id, which is the exact ambiguity the validator exists to prevent.

cases.title: A tag over a 64-code-point astral cycle id
cases.why: This is D2 seen from the tag side: the ledger would accept the lock, and a client counting UTF-16 units cannot even build the tag to check it.

groups.note: arccade-trade-wars-entry v1. The adapters live in js/examples/ and are NOT in the published package, so the cases are expressed as the composition a third party would write: canonFields for each nested record, canonList for the sequence, canonDocument for the envelope.

cases.title: A Trade Wars price point as a bare nested record
cases.why: Nested records inside a list carry no schema wrapper, so a client that wraps each price point in a document produces a different entry digest for the same market snapshot.

pins.daml: canonFields [("as-of", canonTime (addRelTime (time (date 1970 Jan 1) 0 0 0) (microseconds 1000000))), ("price", canonDecimal 60000.0), ("source", canonText "binance"), ("symbol", canonText "BTC")] === "r:95:k:5:as-of=m:7:1000000;k:5:price=d:15:600000000000000;k:6:source=t:7:binance;k:6:symbol=t:3:BTC;"

cases.title: A Trade Wars allocation as a bare nested record
cases.why: The allocation percent is an amount and goes through canonDecimal, not canonText; a client that formats it as a string produces a document that looks right and hashes differently.

cases.title: The Trade Wars golden entry document
cases.why: This digest is asserted in the Daml test suite and is the entry commitment of the first TestNet cycle; it is one of the two constants that bind the game adapters across all four implementations.

cases.title: Swapping two allocations changes the entry digest
cases.why: Allocations are a list, and lists are positional; a client that sorts them to be helpful produces a different commitment for the same portfolio and the cycle can never be settled against it.

cases.title: An entry with no allocations at all
cases.why: A player who commits without allocating anything is a legal cycle, and the empty list has to encode as a counted empty list rather than as nothing.

cases.title: A price point whose as-of has microsecond precision
cases.why: The golden vector uses a whole second so nothing catches a millisecond conversion today; this price point differs in its last three digits, which is exactly the divergence D3 is about.

pins.daml: canonFields [("as-of", canonTime (addRelTime (time (date 1970 Jan 1) 0 0 0) (microseconds 1787605091258920))), ("price", canonDecimal 60000.0), ("source", canonText "binance"), ("symbol", canonText "BTC")] === "r:105:k:5:as-of=m:16:1787605091258920;k:5:price=d:15:600000000000000;k:6:source=t:7:binance;k:6:symbol=t:3:BTC;"

cases.title: An ISO timestamp on a document path must keep its microseconds
cases.why: A strict parser keeps the microseconds while the JavaScript canonTime routes through Date.parse and drops them to ...258000; the two write different Trade Wars entry documents for the same price snapshot, and the same client already parses the instant correctly through isoToMicros.

cases.title: A Trade Wars outcome document
cases.why: The outcome is what settlement commits to, and every one of its amount fields goes through canonDecimal; a client that mixes an integer field in produces an outcome digest the stake will not accept.

cases.title: An outcome with a negative virtual PnL
cases.why: Losses are the outcomes a player disputes, and a negative amount is where a client that truncates away from zero produces a different unit count than the ledger.

cases.title: The golden entry digest is the one inside the TestNet custody tag
cases.why: The entry document, its digest, the custody tag and the audit row all have to agree or the chain from the published document to the ledger has a gap in it; this is the case that closes the loop.

groups.note: arccade-pixel-race-entry v1 and its outcome. Same composition route as Trade Wars, and the seed commitment is a plain textDigest comparison rather than a separate primitive.

cases.title: The Pixel Race golden entry document
cases.why: The second of the two constants the Daml test suite asserts; together with the Trade Wars one it is what makes a claim of adapter parity checkable rather than asserted.

cases.title: A Pixel Race play as a bare nested record
cases.why: Every field of a play is an integer and goes through canonInt; a client that treats the score as an amount multiplies it by 1e10 and the outcome digest stops matching.

pins.daml: canonFields [("coins-collected", canonInt 17), ("game-number", canonInt 1), ("max-level", canonInt 4), ("score", canonInt 9120), ("survival-seconds", canonInt 83)] === "r:119:k:15:coins-collected=i:2:17;k:11:game-number=i:1:1;k:9:max-level=i:1:4;k:5:score=i:4:9120;k:16:survival-seconds=i:2:83;"

cases.title: A Pixel Race outcome with three plays
cases.why: The plays are a positional list and the amounts are decimals, so this one document exercises both conventions at once in the order a real session produces them.

cases.title: An outcome with no plays at all
cases.why: A session where the player never started is a legal outcome, and the empty list has to encode as a counted empty list or the document collides with one whose single play encoded to nothing.

cases.title: Reordering plays changes the list encoding
cases.why: A client that sorts plays by score to make a nicer report changes the outcome digest and the settlement it was committed to no longer matches.

cases.title: The revealed seed hashes to the commitment made at entry
cases.why: The entry commits to a seed hash and the outcome reveals the seed; if the two do not line up the game could pick its randomness after seeing the play, which is the whole thing this commitment prevents.
cases.note: seedMatchesCommit is textDigest(seed) === commit; it needs no capability of its own.

cases.title: An entry whose seed commitment is a real digest
cases.why: The golden entry uses an all-zero commitment, which would also be produced by a client that forgot to hash anything; a real digest is what distinguishes the two.

cases.title: The Pixel Race entry digest that is in the TestNet fixture
cases.why: Two of the three published rows carry this digest inside their custody tags; being able to name the document that produced it is the difference between a hash and a commitment.
cases.note: The fixture digest fd8d8db1... comes from the entry the venue actually published; this case pins the composition route, not that particular preimage.

cases.title: The session cap is an integer field, not an amount
cases.why: max-games-per-session is a count; a client that runs it through canonDecimal writes i-versus-d in the document and every entry digest in the game changes.

cases.title: A tier name containing an emoji
cases.why: Tier names are player-facing and get emoji; this is the shortest path from a product decision to a UTF-16 length bug in a commitment.

groups.note: Fungible and unique instruments, the attribute document that binds a stat sheet to a digest, and the amount rule that keeps "three of this particular sword" from existing.

cases.title: A fungible instrument id
cases.why: Type-level assets are named tenant slash local with no instance part; a client that appends an empty instance separator produces an id that parses back as unique with an empty instance.

cases.title: A unique instrument id
cases.why: Each instance is its own instrument, which is what lets a particular sword carry its own attributes; the separator is what tells the two classes apart at parse time.

cases.title: A three-character instance id is refused
cases.why: Instance ids are derived from attribute digests and truncating one too far makes collisions between different instances likely, which would merge two players items.

cases.title: An uppercase instance id is refused
cases.why: Instrument ids are compared as exact strings on the ledger, so allowing two spellings of the same instance would let the same item exist twice.

cases.title: Parsing a fungible instrument id
cases.why: The parse decides which isolation and amount rules apply, so getting the class wrong means a unique item can be transferred in quantity.

cases.title: Parsing a unique instrument id
cases.why: The instance part is everything after the first separator, so a client splitting on the last one mangles any instance id that happens to contain the separator character.

cases.title: Parsing an instrument id with no namespace
cases.why: Canton Coin has no tenant prefix, and a client that refuses it cannot price a single marketplace trade in the ecosystem currency.

cases.title: A unique instrument is recognised as unique
cases.why: This predicate gates the amount rule below, so it needs its own case rather than being inferred from the rejection it causes.

cases.title: A fungible instrument is not unique
cases.why: The negative case is what stops an implementation from marking everything unique and refusing every quantity above one.

cases.title: Three of one particular sword is refused
cases.why: Quantity on an instance-level asset is meaningless and, if it passed, would show up downstream as something that looks like a double spend.

cases.title: Exactly one of a unique asset is accepted
cases.why: Without the accepting case the rule could be satisfied by refusing every unique asset outright, which would make instance-level items unusable.

cases.title: A zero amount is refused for a fungible asset
cases.why: A zero-amount leg moves nothing while still consuming a write and counting as activity, which is the cheapest way to manufacture volume.

cases.title: A negative amount is refused for a fungible asset
cases.why: A negative leg would reverse the direction of a transfer while the document still reads as a payment to the receiver.

cases.title: An attribute document with an integer and a text attribute
cases.why: Binding the attribute digest to the instrument is what lets a buyer check that a sword really is plus nine and stops the application quietly nerfing it after the sale.

cases.title: A fractional attribute has to be given as text
cases.why: There is no decimal attribute type, so a weight of 1.5 goes in as a string; a client that accepts a float here writes an attribute document whose value depends on the language it was written in.

cases.title: A native float attribute is refused
cases.why: Accepting one would make the same stat sheet hash differently in two languages, and the attribute digest is the only thing a marketplace has to check the item against.

cases.title: The same attributes derive the same instance id
cases.why: Determinism is the point: two mints of the same item get the same id, so an accidental double mint is visible instead of producing two items that look distinct.

cases.title: A salt changes the derived instance id
cases.why: Deliberate reprints need to be distinguishable from accidental ones, and the salt is the only thing separating them; if it did not reach the digest the feature would be a no-op.

cases.title: A different attribute value derives a different instance id
cases.why: If the attributes did not reach the id, a plus-three and a plus-nine sword would share an instance and the marketplace could not tell them apart.

groups.note: Isolation, namespacing and keys. Tenants share one participant and one registry party, so isolation is this layer's responsibility rather than the ledger's.

cases.title: A tenant key hashes to a plain sha256
cases.why: Only the hash is stored server-side, so an implementation that salts or encodes differently cannot verify a key issued by another.

cases.title: The tenant id is readable from the key
cases.why: Routing needs the tenant before verification, and reading it from the key is what lets the lookup happen without a database round trip; it is not a substitute for verifying.

cases.title: A key without the ags_ prefix yields no tenant
cases.why: An unrecognised credential must resolve to nothing rather than to a plausible-looking tenant id that would then be used for a namespace check.

cases.title: A key with no separator yields no tenant
cases.why: A truncated key would otherwise read as a tenant id made of the whole remainder, which could accidentally match a real tenant.

cases.title: A key carrying an invalid tenant id yields no tenant
cases.why: The id inside a key is attacker-controlled text, so it goes through the same validator as any other tenant id rather than being trusted because it arrived in a key.

cases.title: A key verifies against its own hash
cases.why: The value behaviour is in scope even though the constant-time property is not; without the accepting case the rejections could be satisfied by always returning false.

cases.title: A different key does not verify
cases.why: One character difference has to fail, and this is the case that says the comparison is over the hash rather than over the prefix.

cases.title: A hash of the wrong length does not verify
cases.why: A truncated expected hash must be refused rather than compared byte by byte until it runs out, which is both wrong and the shape of a timing leak.

cases.title: A tenant may touch an asset in its own namespace
cases.why: The isolation check runs on every tenant call, so the accepting path is on the hot path and has to be pinned as tightly as the rejection.

cases.title: A tenant may not touch another tenant asset
cases.why: Every tenant item sits under the same registry party, so without this check tenant A could mint or move tenant B item by naming it; the ledger cannot tell them apart.

cases.title: A tenant may touch an asset with no namespace
cases.why: Canton Coin belongs to no tenant, and a client that refuses it cannot take a stake or pay out at all, which would make isolation and usability mutually exclusive.

cases.title: Every leg of a trade is checked, not only the first
cases.why: A two-leg trade where only the offer is in the tenant namespace is exactly how isolation would be bypassed if the check stopped at the first leg.

groups.note: tradeDocument and transferDocument. These are the one place in the SDK where a document is joined with pipes and carries NO length prefixes, which is why the pipe has to be refused inside a component.

cases.title: A marketplace sale as a trade document
cases.why: Only the digest reaches the ledger, so the document has to be reproducible from the published record or a buyer cannot check that the trade they saw is the trade that settled.

cases.title: Legs are ordered by their key, not by insertion
cases.why: The two legs arrive from a map whose iteration order is not fixed across languages, so without the sort the same trade hashes differently depending on who built it.
cases.note: Same expected text as trade-document-two-legs; the identity is the assertion.

cases.title: Meta entries are ordered by their key
cases.why: Meta is caller-supplied and arrives as a map, so it needs the same sort as the legs or two clients building the same trade produce two digests.

cases.title: An open offer writes an empty taker rather than omitting the field
cases.why: Omitting the field would make an open offer and a trade to a party named nothing produce the same bytes, and the document has no length prefixes to tell them apart.

cases.title: A pipe inside a meta value is refused
cases.why: The v1 format joins components with pipes and has no length prefixes, so a pipe inside a value silently reshapes the document into one with an extra component; assertValidTradeId already forbids the character in the id, so the guard is half built.

cases.title: A pipe inside a party name is refused
cases.why: Party ids are ledger-controlled today but the document builder does not know that, and the same ambiguity applies to any component, not only to meta.

cases.title: A leg from a party to itself is refused
cases.why: A self leg moves nothing while still counting as a settled trade, which is the cheapest way to manufacture marketplace volume.

cases.title: A leg of zero is refused
cases.why: A zero leg makes a trade that settles without moving value, which would let a marketplace report activity it never had.

cases.title: A well formed leg is accepted and normalised
cases.why: The amount is normalised to text on the way through, which is what keeps a float from reaching the document; the accepting case is where that normalisation is visible.

cases.title: A single-recipient transfer document
cases.why: The reason classifies the movement in reporting and is inside the hashed text, so a client that leaves it out cannot reproduce the digest that reached the ledger.

cases.title: Recipients keep the order they were given in
cases.why: Recipients are a list, not a map, and are deliberately not sorted; a client that sorts them changes the digest of every batch payout.

cases.title: Transfer meta is sorted while recipients are not
cases.why: The two halves of the same document follow opposite rules on purpose, and a client applying one rule to both gets a different digest for every transfer that carries meta.

cases.title: A pipe inside transfer meta is refused
cases.why: Same ambiguity as the trade document and the same fix; a memo field is the most likely place for a caller to put arbitrary text.

cases.title: A leg with no receiver is refused
cases.why: A leg without both parties cannot be allocated, and the failure would otherwise arrive from the ledger as a missing-field error long after the proposal was published.

cases.title: A leg whose instrument has no admin is refused
cases.why: The admin is the registry that governs the asset, and a leg without one names an asset no registry will settle.

groups.note: Daml Int division truncates TOWARD ZERO and secondsBetween truncates EACH endpoint independently before subtracting. Every policy duration check runs through it, so a client computing (b-a)/1e6 disagrees by up to a second exactly where acceptance flips.

cases.title: Minus seven over two is minus three
cases.why: Floor division would give minus four, and every duration comparison in Policy.daml and Cycle.daml is built on this operator; the sign is where a client that reached for a floor helper diverges.

cases.title: Half a second before the epoch is second zero
cases.why: A floor-based conversion gives minus one, which puts a pre-epoch timestamp in the wrong second; the case is contrived on TestNet and not contrived at all for a client whose clock is wrong.

cases.title: From 0.9s to 60.0s is sixty seconds, not fifty-nine
cases.why: Each endpoint is truncated to whole seconds independently and only then subtracted, so the answer is one more than elapsed time; this is the single most dangerous behaviour in the package because it decides whether a lock or a cycle is long enough.

cases.title: The boundary where policy acceptance flips
cases.why: Elapsed time here is 59.1 seconds and the Daml answer is 60, so a policy with a sixty-second minimum accepts on the ledger and is refused by a client that computes (b-a)/1e6; that is a cycle the game believes it cannot open.
cases.note: Same inputs as the case above, stated from the caller's side. The point is the comparison a client makes, not the arithmetic.

cases.title: Two instants inside one second are zero seconds apart
cases.why: A minimum cycle duration of one second is satisfied by nothing that happens inside the same second, which is what stops a commit and settle in the same instant from counting.

cases.title: One microsecond across a second boundary is one second
cases.why: The mirror of the previous case: almost no elapsed time counts as a full second because both endpoints are truncated first, and a client that rounds instead of truncating gets zero.

cases.title: A backwards interval is negative, not an error
cases.why: Clock skew between a client and the ledger produces exactly this, and a client that takes an absolute value would accept a lock that expires before it starts.

cases.title: A whole second converts exactly
cases.why: The unremarkable case has to be pinned so the negative and fractional ones are a comparison rather than isolated assertions.

cases.title: A fractional second is dropped, not rounded
cases.why: The real TestNet commit timestamp has 372202 microseconds on it, and rounding up would put the cycle in the next second and, at a period boundary, in the next day.

cases.title: A cooldown is added in whole seconds
cases.why: nextEligibleAt is computed this way at settlement, and the commit choice refuses while now is before it; an off-by-a-thousand in the unit makes the cooldown either instant or seventeen minutes.

cases.title: A zero cooldown leaves the instant unchanged
cases.why: A venue may set no cooldown, and a client that treats zero as unset and substitutes a default silently locks players out of a mechanic the venue chose to allow.

cases.title: A negative offset moves the instant backwards
cases.why: Abort uses a different cooldown from settlement and a client could pass the difference; the arithmetic has to be plain rather than clamped at zero, or the two paths stop agreeing.

groups.note: The arithmetic Cycle.daml enforces at settlement. No client re-checks it, so a report can state amounts the ledger would have refused and every individual proof still verifies.

cases.title: A full return is valid
cases.why: This is the disposition on the first published TestNet row, so the accepting case is the one an auditor meets first and it has to be pinned before the rejections mean anything.

cases.title: Returned plus forfeited must equal the stake
cases.why: Any other split either creates value out of nothing or loses some, and the row would still hash and verify perfectly; conservation is the one property a Merkle proof cannot express.

cases.title: A full return cannot forfeit anything
cases.why: The disposition tag is what a player and an auditor read, so a returned-in-full row that also forfeits is a document that contradicts itself while remaining arithmetically balanced.

cases.title: A full forfeit is valid
cases.why: The opposite extreme of the same rule, pinned so the check is a comparison of both sides rather than a one-way test.

cases.title: A full forfeit cannot return anything
cases.why: A row that forfeits in full while returning most of the stake would let a venue report a loss it did not impose, and the amounts would still sum correctly.

cases.title: A partial forfeit needs both sides non-zero
cases.why: returned-with-forfeit is the disposition a player is most likely to dispute, so the tag has to mean what it says rather than being a catch-all for any split.

cases.title: A partial forfeit that forfeits nothing is refused
cases.why: It would be a full return wearing a different label, which matters because the two tags carry different meanings in a dispute and in the reported totals.

cases.title: A negative returned amount is refused
cases.why: A negative leg reverses the direction of the settlement while the row still reads as a payment to the player.

cases.title: A payout above the policy cap is refused
cases.why: The cap is the venue commitment about maximum exposure, and it is enforced on the ledger; a report that states a payout above it describes a settlement that could not have happened.

cases.title: A payout exactly at the cap is accepted
cases.why: The bound is inclusive, and pinning the edge from the accepting side stops the check from drifting into a strict inequality that would refuse the venue own maximum.

cases.title: An aborted cycle returns the stake in full
cases.why: Unlocking a TimeLockedHolding always pays the owner in full and this mechanic cannot forfeit, so an abort row that returns less than the stake describes value that went nowhere.

cases.title: An aborted cycle that returns less than the stake is refused
cases.why: This is how a venue would take a fee out of an abort without saying so, and the row would balance because the difference could be booked as a forfeit.

cases.title: An expired cycle returns the stake in full
cases.why: Expiry is the player unconditional exit and needs neither arCCade nor the DSO, so anything less than a full return would make that exit conditional after all.

cases.title: The settle builder refuses a forfeit on a full return
cases.why: This is the one settlement invariant a shipped client does check, and pinning it says which part of the arithmetic is already guarded and which part is not.

cases.title: The settle builder refuses a return on a full forfeit
cases.why: The mirror guard, and the pair is what shows the check is on both dispositions rather than on whichever one was written first.

groups.note: Wire constants. A rename invalidates every commitment already on the ledger, so each one gets a case; a change arrives as a v2 scheme alongside v1, never as an edit.

cases.title: The SCHEME_PREFIX wire constant
cases.why: The first component of every canonical document; renaming it would orphan every value already written under the old spelling, and the rename would look like a harmless refactor in review.

cases.title: The DIGEST_ALG_ID wire constant

cases.title: The offer leg key
cases.why: Leg keys are sorted into the trade document, so renaming one reorders the document and changes the digest of every trade that has ever been proposed.

cases.title: The reward transfer reason
cases.why: The reason string is inside the hashed transfer document, so it is a wire value and not a display label, which is easy to forget when adding a reason.

groups.note: Per-tenant write quota as a state-machine trace with an INJECTED clock. Deterministic, which is why it is an optional profile rather than an exclusion.

cases.title: Three writes inside the window are allowed and counted down
cases.why: Economic cost is the first defence against spam and the quota is the administrative second; the remaining count is what a caller shows a tenant, so it is part of the contract, not a debug field.

cases.title: The fourth write in a window is refused
cases.why: A client that allows the cap-plus-one write makes the quota advisory, and a well funded tenant can then produce operationally harmful volume that is economically legitimate.

cases.title: The window rolls at exactly windowSeconds, not one millisecond later
cases.why: The comparison is greater-or-equal, so the write at exactly the boundary starts a fresh window; an implementation using a strict comparison holds a tenant out for one extra millisecond every window forever.

cases.title: A single call may cost more than one write
cases.why: The two-write cycle costs two, so a client that always charges one lets a tenant open twice as many cycles as its quota allows.

cases.title: A cost above the cap can never be allowed
cases.why: Otherwise a caller could get an oversized batch through by waiting for a fresh window, which would make the cap a rate rather than a bound.

cases.title: resetAt is the start of the window plus its length
cases.why: Callers surface resetAt to tenants as a retry-after, so a client computing it from the current instant instead of the window start tells every tenant to retry too late.

cases.title: One tenant cannot spend another tenant quota
cases.why: A shared bucket would let a noisy tenant deny service to a quiet one on the same participant, which is the isolation failure this layer exists to prevent.

cases.title: A refused write does not eat quota
cases.why: If refusals consumed the budget a tenant that retries would never recover inside the window, turning a rate limit into a lockout.

cases.title: The quota check validates the tenant id
cases.why: The tenant id arrives from a key that is attacker-controlled text, and an unvalidated one would create an unbounded number of buckets, each with a full allowance.

cases.title: A fresh window restores the full allowance
cases.why: A client that decays the counter instead of resetting it gives a tenant less than its stated quota, and the difference only shows under sustained load.

groups.note: Ledger command payloads. Only the JavaScript client builds them, and excluding them because of that would be exactly the quiet stop this suite exists to prevent: the output is deterministic JSON, so it is checkable.

cases.title: Write one is exactly two commands in a single submission
cases.why: Sent apart, a GameStake can exist unfunded or a lock can exist with no cycle behind it; the atomicity is the entire reason the commit builder exists rather than two calls.

cases.title: The custody tag is written into the lock optContext
cases.why: The two commands cannot see each other, so the tag in optContext is the only thing binding the lock to the cycle; a generic string there makes the stake unsettleable and abortable only.

cases.title: A zero fee produces no fee output
cases.why: An output of zero would be a transfer leg that moves nothing and still costs a ledger write, and dry-run mode requires the fee to be zero, so this path is on the learning ramp.

cases.title: An omitted fee amount is refused, not serialised
cases.why: Bare String() serialisation sends the literal text undefined to the ledger as the fee, which was verified against a live submission; the ledger then rejects it with a parse error that says nothing about the missing field.

cases.title: A commit with no Amulet inputs is refused
cases.why: There would be nothing to lock, and the transfer command would be built anyway; the failure would surface as a ledger rejection with no indication of which field was empty.

cases.title: A commit with a colon in the cycle id is refused
cases.why: The builder is where the identifier rules are actually enforced for most callers, so a validator that is never reached from a builder protects nothing.

cases.title: A commit with a malformed entry digest is refused
cases.why: The entry digest goes straight into the custody tag, so a malformed one produces a tag that settlement can never re-derive and a stake that can only be aborted.

cases.title: A dry-run commit is a single command with no lock
cases.why: The learning ramp has to run without Canton Coin or disclosed contracts from Scan; if dry run needed the transfer half, the first hour would be spent on Splice transfer mechanics rather than on the SDK.

cases.title: A dry-run commit writes a zero fee explicitly
cases.why: Mode discipline enforces a zero fee on the ledger, and writing it explicitly means a caller who expected to charge one finds out here rather than in a rejection from the venue contract.

cases.title: Settle comes before the unlock, never after
cases.why: GameStake_Settle reads the lock through the Holding interface, so the unlock that archives it has to come second; reversed, settlement is refused for having no custody proof.

cases.title: A settlement with no lock is a single command
cases.why: Dry-run cycles and cycles whose unlock rides in another transaction have no locked Amulet to archive, and a builder that always emits two commands makes those submissions fail.

cases.title: An outcome document is hashed into the outcome digest
cases.why: Callers pass the document and expect the digest to be derived from it; a client that requires both invites them to drift apart, and the digest is what the ledger stores.

cases.title: A settlement with neither a document nor a digest is refused
cases.why: The outcome commitment is the whole point of settlement; without it the row would carry an empty outcome that reads exactly like a legitimate abort.

cases.title: An abort takes its custody reference optionally
cases.why: The reason abort exists is that the lock may never have been created, so requiring the reference would make the escape hatch unusable in exactly the case it was built for.

cases.title: Expiry is submitted by the player alone
cases.why: It is the unconditional exit: after the lock expires the player recovers both the funds and the slot without arCCade or the DSO, and any extra actAs party would reintroduce the dependency.

cases.title: A trade proposal carries the digest of its own document
cases.why: Only the digest reaches the ledger, so a proposal whose digest was computed from different inputs than the published document cannot be checked by the buyer at all.

cases.title: A trade with only an offer is refused
cases.why: A one-sided trade is a transfer wearing a trade label, and it would settle atomically while moving value in only one direction.

cases.title: Settling a trade with no allocations is refused
cases.why: Every leg needs its allocation contract id for the settlement to be atomic; an empty map would submit a settle that can only fail on the ledger.

cases.title: Cancelling a trade is one command from the venue
cases.why: Allocation withdrawal is what makes a trade cancellable without escrow, and the cancel path has to stay a single venue-signed command or the counterparty could block it.

cases.title: A batch payout is one command, not one per recipient
cases.why: Splitting a payout into N transactions would inflate the qualifying-activity count for the same economic event, and the builder deliberately does not make that easy.

cases.title: An unknown transfer reason is refused
cases.why: The reason is inside the hashed document, so an unrecognised one produces a digest no other client reproduces and a report category nothing else understands.

cases.title: A transfer to the sender is refused
cases.why: It is the cheapest way to manufacture volume that looks like real activity, and it is closed at the source rather than left to a reporting filter.

cases.title: The same recipient twice in one batch is refused
cases.why: Paying one party twice in a single transaction is one payment split in two, which inflates the recipient count in a report without moving any more value.

cases.title: A transfer with no recipients is refused
cases.why: It would submit a transfer command with no outputs, burning a write and a fee to move nothing.

cases.title: A zero-amount recipient is refused
cases.why: A zero leg is a payment that moves nothing while still counting as one, and the batch would otherwise succeed with it silently included.

cases.title: A commit with a 65-character cycle id is refused
cases.why: The length bound and the forbidden-character rule are separate checks with separate messages, and a builder that reaches only one of them lets the other kind of bad id through to the ledger.
